nodes.text: THE EXPOSITIONS OF SAINT MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF TURIN, ON CHAPTERS OF THE GOSPELS.
ADMONITION.

Long ago Gennadius, in the Catalogue which he was the first to compile, had noted of the works of St Maximus of Turin that he had expounded many things wisely on chapters of the Gospels and of the Acts of the Apostles; and after him John Trithemius, a most learned Benedictine monk and another recorder of Maximus' works, made mention in the first place of the Chapters on the Gospels. Until now those chapters have lain so buried in darkness that none of the later writers recalled them, nor has any of the commentators on the sacred Scriptures given any sign that he had approved or seen them. Some hope, however, had shone on us that St Thomas, who put together a Catena from the opinions of the Fathers on the four Gospels, cites some interpretations of Maximus. He does indeed have several, especially on Luke, but he did not draw them from the Chapters with which we are dealing. Yet this silence of a later age does not prevent us from asserting that Maximus is the author of these Chapters. For it is established that in the course of time many writings of the Fathers have been discovered which lay hidden in old manuscripts and awaited the care and diligence of more recent critics. In editing these Sirmond, Mabillon, Leo Allatius, Luc d'Achery, and the Benedictine monks of the congregation of St Maur, to omit a great many others, have won distinction, and have fortified the doctrine of the Church with great safeguards. For our part, besides those two testimonies of Gennadius and Trithemius, we are moved by reasons which carry no slight weight with us. First, we meet the same themes that Maximus treated in his homilies and sermons. 2. The constant use of the old Itala version of the divine Books, which is consistent in Maximus. 3. The admirable linking of the sacred Scriptures; and whether he explains the literal or the mystical sense, he shows not only a perfect understanding of the word of God but also a singular sharpness of mind. 4. The style of the Expositions, which, although we find it plainer, nevertheless displays very many of his ways of speaking, so that they seem to have flowed from the same vein. 5. Finally we add their singular agreement with Maximus, whether you take his homilies or his treatises; which would be very difficult to bring about if another mind and hand had been at work. These chapters have come down to us interpolated in various places from the Verona codex marked no. 49, owing to its age; but we have filled some gaps from the passages of Scripture indicated. We have moreover corrected not a few errors of the copyist, which must be forgiven to the antiquity of the times, so that as far as lay in us we might render a purer and more complete text. We hope to do something welcome to those devoted to sacred studies in offering them for consultation St Maximus, who deserved so well of the Interpretation of the Gospels. Perhaps someone will arise who will rescue from oblivion the same Maximus' Expositions on the Acts of the Apostles.
I. On the readings of the holy Gospels, Mark 6:38.

Today it was read in the holy Gospel that the Lord Jesus in the desert fed five thousand men from five loaves and two fishes. Everywhere the Lord Jesus heals all, feeds all; with him the blind find eyes, from him the deaf receive hearing, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, demons are put to flight, paralytics, their limbs loosened, are made firm again; the lame run with firm steps, and all glory in his gifts; even the waters of the sea and the swelling waves, their motions fixed in themselves, revere him as he walks [on them] with servile obedience. So today, as was read, five thousand men are fed by the Lord from five loaves and two fishes, and twelve baskets full of fragments are gathered. Let us consider, brothers, the wonders of the Lord Jesus. He touches the loaves, and as he multiplies the rains upon the earth, so everything grows into an abundant multitude. The bread receives increase, and in wondrous ways among the crowds of those eating a white harvest of fragments springs up. All are filled, the peoples are fed; twelve full baskets are still gathered, according to the number of the twelve beloved disciples, so that the Church may always abound in the truth (fruitfulness) of the apostles and be fed with the loaves of their teaching. And so on.
II.

Likewise on the reading of the holy Gospel, or on the chapter where the Lord says, John 7:28: Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink; whoever believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.

Rightly did the most holy prophet David, held in suspense by a religious thirst and burning with great ardour, say to him whom he saw in the spirit: As the hart longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God (Ps. 41). With such ardour burned also that blessed Mary, the sister of Martha, whom the Lord nourished with sacred words [...] in no way did she withdraw [...] this good woman without doubt held the part which could never be taken from her. For she could never lose what the Lord by his kindness had granted her to possess, since he himself gives spiritual water to the thirsty, he who said today: Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7). This Mary, then, of whom we made mention, seems to me to represent the faithful Church, which prefers to cleave to the Lord, which the Lord always builds up by his speech, which is drenched by frequent floods from the springs of Christ, which, sitting by him and cleaving to his footsteps, the Lord does not spurn but rather consoles; he who also deigned to wash the feet of the disciples, so that what Abraham had once done for him, he himself took care to show to the sons of Abraham. Does it not seem to you, I ask, that this Mary sitting at the Lord's feet [...] we say to lose the person [...] In the Psalms the divine word speaks: Hear, daughter, incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house; and the king will desire your beauty, for he is the Lord your God, and you shall worship him (Ps. 44). So the Church, as has been said, is watered from the springs of Christ. For the Lord Christ loves and has loved the Church, as the Apostle proves, saying: Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water in the word of life (Eph. 5), etc. So, whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Let us drink, I beseech you, brothers, those heavenly waters coming from the springs of Christ, and let us sing to the same Lord of ours a new song. For let the renewed people of the Church sing a new song too. Let us walk singing psalms on the royal road, that we may come to the Father of the Lord. You say to me: What is this royal road? Hear the Saviour himself saying: I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14). It is called the royal road because he is our king; and the prophet says: O God, give your judgement to the king, and your justice to the king's son (Ps. 71). This is the royal road, this is the spring of life from which, while we live, the soul receives its fill of all good things. Again the prophet spoke in the person of the Lord himself, saying: Come, sons, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord (Ps. 33). Come, sons. He says 'sons', because as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God (John 1). So: come, sons, hear me; come to me, the way, that, freed from the errors and windings of the world, you may proceed by a straight road to the Father. I am, he says, the way, in which there are no twisting turns of crimes, no malice of perversity, no stony, no thorny places; but all is clear, all pleasant, all harmless and safe, where the footsteps of the faithful soul are not hurt. There is nothing, brothers, harsh with the Lord, nothing to shudder at with Christ, where fatherly mercy has prepared everything pleasant. So in his person the evangelist (Matt. 9) teaches that it is better to enter the kingdom of God with one eye, one hand and one foot, than having two eyes, two hands and two feet to be sent into the gehenna of fire, where their worm shall not die and the fire shall not be quenched. Whoever hears this is without doubt terrified, and would that he were terrified more strongly; for by fearing the divine commands he is freed from sin; for the fear of God, as Scripture says, drives out sin (Sir. 1). For whoever is without fear cannot be justified; so if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you (Matt. 5); for it is better to bear a wound of the body than to suffer the shipwreck of chastity, where the soul will perish together with the body. But lest this cutting off trouble you, whoever you are, with a frail understanding, so that you think you ought to amputate the limbs of your body, and the most necessary ones at that: the Lord commanded that not limbs, plainly, but vices be cut away, and all the motions and impulses of sins be broken, so that where the enemy drives the mind toward the precipice of damnation, there, as the wall of chastity resists him, his devices of sin may perish. If your right eye causes you to stumble, that is, if with unlawful intent you delight to see what can kill, and to prepare swords for yourself with curious eyes, when you ought rather with praiseworthy modesty to guard your eyes with your very fingers, and, covered with the comely veil of chastity, not let them loose to any wanton vices, but seize, as was said, your very sight and subject it to the reins of divine strength; lest the soldier of Christ be conquered by the loose enticements of thoughts, or the chaste woman be held by playful eyes in serpentine coils. These things are to be guarded against, dearest ones. I am, says the Lord, the light of the world; whoever follows me will not remain in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8). Let us therefore choose, dearest ones, the bright light rather than the error of darkness, so that, remaining in the light, by the help of the light, they may be filled with the common joy of a good conscience, always giving thanks to the Lord, who is blessed for ever. Amen.
III. Likewise, it was read in the holy Gospel, Mark 4:14: He who speaks sows the word.

Hence, dearest ones, let us speak about the Lord's saying, with the Lord himself helping us: He who speaks sows the word. It is most certain that he who speaks sows the word; he scatters words like seeds, but God gives the increase. For take a comparison: when seed is held in the hand, it remains by itself alone; but if it has been cast, and once sown has been soaked with heavenly rain, by divine Providence it takes root and grows. So too with us: while we hold the word in our mouth, it remains by itself alone; but if it has been cast, and in a manner sown, by the grace of God it takes root in the hearts of each person, and grows, and is multiplied in fruits. Therefore it was rightly said: He who speaks sows the word. And hear what fruits the seed of God, the spiritual word, bears: But the fruits of the spirit, he says, are hope, love, joy, peace (Gal. 5), and the rest. The earth of the heart that receives the Lord's seed bears fruits that are joyful both in body and in spirit. Hence the apostle Paul too said to his hearers: We have sown spiritual things for you; is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things (1 Cor. 9)? Therefore let the field of our breast be made fertile, so that it may receive the Lord's seed and enrich [us] with a fertile crop; let there be no thorns and thistles of worldly ill will in the earth of our heart, lest a harmful growth kill the good seed; let there be no stony places in you, and no barren ruin of stones. For the Lord, who says, I will dwell in them and walk among them (2 Cor. 6), shudders at such a road; but let the earth of our heart be, as I said, good, which bears fruit thirtyfold, and sixtyfold, and a hundredfold; that is, let it be multiplied in all good things, let it have in itself fruits of grain, wine and oil. The fruit of wine, that is, the faith and confession of the passion and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, who washed his robe in wine and his covering in the blood of the grape (Gen. 49), and drenched the winepress of the vintage with saving ardour: those who live by the sacrament of his cup are so intoxicated with his spiritual ardour that they do not feel the storms of the world, nor injuries, nor the punishments of persecutors; so that they proclaim and say: And your intoxicating cup, how glorious it is (Ps. 22). Therefore, the fruits of grain, wine and oil. The fruits of oil are gladness, peace, sweetness, serenity of mind, which, like oil, floats on top and rises above; hence the head too is commanded to be anointed, so that the head of our heart may shine with that brightness. Let our mind therefore always abound in these spiritual goods, so that we may always give thanks to the Father through the Son. Amen.
IV. Likewise, on the reading of the holy Gospel, Mark 6:31.

It was read that, after John the Baptist was killed by the impious Herod, the Lord told his disciples to cross over to a deserted place and rest a little. John was killed by Herod, a holy man by a wicked one, a kind man by an impious one; but let the enemy not rejoice, for the just man, by whatever death he is overtaken, will be in refreshment (Wis. 4). Rightly did the prophet say, How much evil the enemy has done among his saints (Ps. 73). And he is ordered to be killed at a banquet. What will luxurious banquets not drive mortal hearts to? What will drunken revels not force reckless minds to do? O crime! Amid the pouring of wine, the pouring of a just man's blood is demanded. It was not enough for unspeakable lust that such great luxury was carried on at the banquet: a holy man is killed. A wanton girl by dancing enticed the mind of impious Herod. She had learned from her impious mother to pursue shamelessness. Such a girl pleased Herod, to whom luxury could be more pleasing than to an adulterer. The devil found a craft by which to kill the man of God, so as to slaughter the accuser of luxury by luxury itself. But the wretch does not know that precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Ps. 115). So precious is it that by dying it possesses eternal life. Now the Lord, hearing about John, went away to a deserted place with his disciples. He gathered his flock to himself, lest they be harassed by the savagery of wolves; lest Herod, the persecutor of justice, should again find people to destroy. He crosses to the desert, to refuse the company of the impious and to display the wonders of his mighty works. For the desert signifies the Church, which did not yet have the tillage of the apostles nor the crops of the divine word, but was still rough and untilled with the brambles of vices and ignorance. Of it was said: Rejoice, thirsty wilderness, for many are the children of the deserted woman, more than of her who has a husband (Isa. 54). The Lord Jesus came there, he multiplies five loaves, so that the Church of God might abound in the manifold gifts of divine grace. Those five loaves which are multiplied we can understand as the five bodily senses, which are multiplied in spiritual senses. The two fish [are] the New and Old Testament, by which people are nourished, but together with bread, that is, with Christ, who is the bread of life. So he blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before them, and divided the two fish among all (Mark 6); and increases of the bread follow, and the fish are likewise multiplied, five thousand men are filled with the sweetness of Christ's gifts. And they still gather twelve full baskets of fragments; but these twelve baskets show the bright fullness of the twelve disciples; just as in another place too the seven full hampers taken up, sevenfold, showed an image of the Church. For there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church is fortified and renewed. They are listed by the Apostle (1 Cor. 12). This gift, this inheritance, Christ gave to his people, so that whoever follows him may always be filled with heavenly goods from his abundance. Amen.
V. Likewise, on the Gospel reading Matthew 9:18

Where a certain ruler came and worshipped the Lord, saying: Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand on her, and she will live. And the Lord rose and followed him, and so on. [...] of the ruler, brothers. For he said within himself: God sent his Son and gave all things into his hand; and therefore he said: Come, lay your hand on her, and she will live. Christ, the Life, brings the dead to life, heals the sick, cleanses lepers, drives out demons, strengthens paralytics, gives the lame the power to walk, gives light to the blind, and does many wonders. The girl had died and had already, at that very moment, departed to the abodes below. But the girl's devoted father, seeing her bloodless limbs, begged the protection of the Lord Christ against the ruin and plunder of death. And the most merciful Lord gladly heard the petitioner's request. And rising, he followed him. It says rising; so a little before he was sitting, waiting to see whether anyone would come to ask for benefits. Rising, he followed him. The father hurried for his one daughter; the Lord too hurried for one handmaid, taking more care for all than each person does for his own. But see, in the crowd [was] a certain woman whom a troublesome illness often afflicted and a flow of blood most violently wasted, and she no longer had strength of body; only faith, all human substance being exhausted, did she keep in her heart, which the Lord's coming had suddenly impressed upon her whole senses. She approached, saying within herself: If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed (Matt. 9). She said this within herself, so that she might be healed within herself the sooner. Christ was present to her as she thought, and at once, at the very touch of the fringe, she is healed. She touched the fringe and obtained a cure, and through the comfort of a little garment found great health. So the Lord Christ, rewarder of the faithful, grants great things for small. So he came also to the ruler's house, and says to the mourners: The girl is not dead, but sleeps. O Lord Jesus, how is the girl not dead but sleeping, when the spirit of life is not in her? To me, he says, who will raise her, she sleeps; and taking her hand he raised her, and, restoring her alive by the light of his splendour, he entrusted her to her devoted parents in the sight of all. He it is who will bring about the resurrection of all alike: to him be glory for ever. Amen.
VI. Likewise, on the reading of the holy Gospel where a woman is cured of a flow of blood, Matthew 9:20.

Our Lord and Saviour Christ, whose wonderful works we have heard today in the holy Gospel, says: I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14). Let us therefore approach him, brothers, so that, walking through him on so blessed a journey, we may be able to reach the Father. Let us approach him as this woman approached faithfully today, and let us touch [him] by faith. And although the Lord Jesus is always set among crowds, and around him stand not only apostles and prophets, but also martyrs and all the just, and a crowd of angels too and of all the heavenly powers; yet if we touch the fringe of his garment, and through that very clothing, that is, through the veil of the body [...] is the propitiatory [...] we invoke the help of [his] majesty, and work aided by his heavenly gifts; at once we too shall be healed of our infirmity, and the flood of blood, that is, the perilous storm of carnal vices, will not kill us. This faithful woman did this, of whom the holy Gospel told a little before: and let us consider what the person of this woman signifies. This woman, it seems to me, showed in herself a figure of all human frailty, which, previously set in the affliction of the flesh, that is, established in the vices of sins, could not be cured otherwise than by receiving remedies from Christ. Or again she showed in herself an image of the Synagogue, which laboured for a long time in the blood of its members, that is, in the circumcision of its sons. She had spent much, as it were, on physicians, that is, on the scribes and Pharisees, whose false and empty words of doctrine she sought, and was made all the weaker by them. After she saw that Christ had come as Saviour to the nations, she chose the better part, and passed over to faith, and began to think within herself, saying: If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed. And at once, believing, she received God in the body, ran by the strength of faith to Christ, and touching the fringe of his garment received the fullest remedy of salvation from the divine springs. And therefore the Lord said to her: Be steadfast, daughter, your faith has saved you: go in peace; that is, walk secure in peace; reject the wars of the vices that tore your soul apart, and always hold the peace of faith and the fear of God, and be healed of your affliction. Every person had in himself the affliction of sins, not only among the Jews but among the gentiles too; coming to Christ he is saved by him, and through faith is fortified by the help of his blessing: to him be glory and dominion for ever. Amen.
VII. Likewise, on the holy Gospel, Luke 11:27.

When the Lord was speaking to the crowds, and sowing words of devotion and salvation in the hearts of all, a certain woman from the crowd cried out to him and said: Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked. The Lord said to her: Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.

Blessed, she says, is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked. This woman, brothers, moved by a devout feeling, praised the mother's womb, praised the breasts of her who bore him; filled indeed with the Holy Spirit, she rightly bestowed praise of the Lord on the mother who had brought forth such an offspring and had suckled such a child. On this mother the Lord himself had surely conferred a special blessedness in this, that he had chosen her womb for his majesty as a kind of royal house, into which the heavenly King himself might descend. Blessed enough and greatly, and blessed she was found worthy to be, the mother of the Lord, and, taken up from being a handmaid, she received the name of mother. Therefore, blessed, she says, is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked. Blessed the womb that bore the maker of the world, blessed the breasts that suckled the Lord of the world. And the Lord says: Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Those who hear the word of God, that is, Christ the Word of God; and keep it, that is, keep his commandment. The Word of God is Christ the Lord, who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word (John 1). Therefore blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it, that is, [hear] the commandment of God and keep it with careful observance. The highest and perfect blessedness is placed chiefly in this, if what is said is fulfilled. Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it; because with listening ears they preserve the divine words with their whole heart, and show by the works of their deeds that what the divine preaching often commanded has been fulfilled by them. Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it, where it is said: You shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not commit adultery, and you shall not covet, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not swear falsely; honour your father and mother; and what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another; and whatever you wish that people should do to you, do those same good things to them also. Blessed, he says, are those who hear the word of God and keep it, so that by keeping and doing it they may obtain the reward. After this it is related, with the Lord saying: This wicked generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah (Luke 11). This most holy prophet Jonah bore in himself a figure of the Lord's passion and resurrection. Once, when the sailors threw him headlong into the sea, he was received by a whale and, seized in its slimy jaws, entered the gate of the beast's belly, and, held for three days and as many nights in the darkness of that dear prison, at last restored to the light, he showed, as we have said, the future sacraments of the Lord's mystery. The Lord, recalling this very thing, signified by it his own passion and resurrection. And concerning the queen of the South, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (ibid.): let the Jews blush and be confounded; a woman seeks the wisdom of a man, and the scribes and Pharisees despise the wisdom of God. She travels abroad to learn from Solomon the son of David; they despise, present among them, the Lord both of Solomon and of David himself, as David himself says: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand (Ps. 109). Then also concerning the Ninevites, who did penance at the preaching of Jonah: And behold, something more than Jonah is here: the Ninevites did penance when a servant preached, and the Jews, when the Lord preached, despise him and will not do penance, because neither do they deserve to be saved. Truly they are deaf adders that stop their ears (Ps. 57), which do not hear the voice of the charmers, nor of the remedy prepared by the wise; whom the Wisdom of the Father himself, the Lord Christ, though teaching them very often, both through Moses and the other prophets, in no way called back to the right path of life; because he did not wish to break off again the free will that he had given to man, lest he should infringe the freedom of mind he had lately granted, as we have said. Therefore he left it to each person's judgement, reserving to himself the future examination of these things, so that he who is guilty may be punished, and he may be saved who refused to commit a crime, so as not to be punished. And therefore, brothers, in the precept of the divine discourse let us search its words with all the attention of the mind; and to God the Father almighty let us always give praise and thanks through Christ our Lord, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
VIII. Likewise, on the Gospel reading Luke 18:10.

The reading was about the Pharisee and the tax-collector; when I consider the merits, prayers and persons of these two, I greatly marvel at the goodness of God and the just judgement of Christ. Pride was confounded, humility deserved to be justified; tears found mercy, boasting is rejected. The Pharisee, who was rejoicing, blushed; the tax-collector, who was lamenting, rejoiced, and hears [the sentence of] justice; for everyone, says the Lord, who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 18); and those who sow in tears will reap in joy (Ps. 125); the Lord is always near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit (Ps. 33). Let us consider, brothers, the text of this reading. Two men, it says, went up into the temple to pray, a Pharisee and a tax-collector. Well is it said 'they went up' [...] and yet [...] he who raises his mind to God will be justified only in humility. Therefore let us consider: those men went up into the temple to pray. The Pharisee prayed by himself, saying: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, as is also this tax-collector, etc. But the tax-collector stood far off, and would not even raise his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me a sinner. And this tax-collector went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. First, in these two I understand the persons of two peoples to be signified, of the Jews and of the gentiles. So the Pharisee said: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, like this tax-collector. You would do well to give thanks [...] you do not accuse at all [...] you would do well if you had not lifted [yourself] up with proud words; for when you accuse others, you condemn yourself, because you ascribe praise to yourself from the faults of others; do not be high-minded, but fear. God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, as is also this tax-collector. Who are you to judge another's servant? To his own master he stands or falls. God is able to make him stand (Rom. 14). Further you say: I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess; in one's own praise boasting is odious. I fast twice in the week: let him who fasts not judge him who eats, and let him who eats not despise him who fasts; for he who eats, eats to the Lord, and gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, abstains to the Lord, and gives thanks to God (ibid.); and yet, to whom do you say these things? Do you not understand that you are speaking to him to whom all things are known, even before they happen? I give tithes of all that I possess. You give tithes, but you receive more than you give: you possess too much; your many crops grow for you by divine rains, and to him to whom you give a little out of much, you still make reproaches. But the tax-collector stood far off, bearing, as we have said, the person of the gentiles, because the gentiles were held further away from God by their sins. So he stood far off, and would not even raise his eyes to heaven. You see, the conscience of the petitioner now becomes its own judge; it punishes sins in itself, does not dare approach nearer, does not dare raise its eyes to heaven, nor wishes to look with polluted eyes on the bright light, because clear light dazzles and strikes eyes that are in pain; and therefore, bowed towards the earth, he beat his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me a sinner. And the Lord said: Amen I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than that Pharisee; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted. And therefore let us too, brothers, pursue humility, and with a gentle heart and humble prayer entreat the Lord, that we may obtain the help of his mercy, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
IX. Likewise, on the Gospel reading Matthew 21:1.

The Lord Jesus sent disciples to bring him the colt of an ass, on which he might sit; and the disciples went. When they found the colt tied, they untied it and led it to the Saviour, and he sat upon it. Hear, brothers: the true prophecy of holy Isaiah has been fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ; for so the prophet Isaiah himself, full of the Holy Spirit, spoke of the Saviour, saying: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion: behold, your King comes to you, meek and gentle, sitting upon the colt of an ass (Isa. 62; Zech. 9). What do we say, brothers? First we must marvel at such great humility of the Lord; knowing that the pomp of the world is superfluous, he took no delight in horses snorting with proud necks, nor stepping with high paces, but chose to be carried on the back of a lowly colt, showing that he loves not the proud and self-exalting, but the meek and those as it were lowly, who are held like the refuse of the world; for, as the Apostle says: God chose the ignoble things of this world to confound the strong, and God chose the despised things, which are not, to destroy the things that are (1 Cor. 1). So the disciples bring the colt of an ass, untying it. Here, beloved, there is a great mystery. This colt of an ass is understood as the people of the gentiles, which was held lowly and despised, and was kept bound by the chains of sins; it is untied by the disciples, sent by the Lord's command for the salvation and freedom of the nations, and is led to the service of the Saviour, that is, to the mystery of faith, so that it may carry the Lord in itself, and he may rest and dwell in it; he being about to make, by his dignity, out of a most lowly rabble a most precious people, a royal and priestly race, so that he may order their formerly sluggish minds by a watchful precept, and submit them to the honourable yoke of devotion, so that they may serve him, and those in whom the Lord sits may be honoured by the rest, just as today we see religious people, who bear Christ in themselves and hold his discipline in their conduct, honoured in the Lord's honour by the other peoples. Thanks be to God.
X. Likewise, on the reading of the holy Gospel, Matthew 14:20.

The reading has been recited in which the Saviour satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes, and twelve full baskets were gathered up. Then [it was read] that again he satisfied four thousand men with seven loaves, and seven hampers full of fragments were gathered up. A man who was dumb and deaf is also healed: The Lord spat, and touched his tongue, and put his fingers into his ears; and looking up to heaven he groaned, and said: Ephphatha, that is, be opened; and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and his ears were opened, and he spoke rightly (Mark 7). He also heals a blind man by laying on his hands, and performs other mighty works of healing. Everywhere, brothers, Christ the Lord is health for all: he feeds all, heals all, gives life to all, comes to the aid of all, has mercy on all, since he is God of all creation, who, sent by the Father, deigned to heal the sufferings of his own image, removing the various torment of diseases. He blesses the loaves and likewise the fishes, to show that he is the maker of land and sea, who by divine bounty grants all things both on land and in the waters. Twelve baskets and seven full hampers are gathered up, so that both the number of the apostles and [the number] of the Churches may be known to overflow with the bounty of Christ. Then a man who was dumb and deaf is healed; two weak members receive medicine. The Lord spat, and touched his tongue, put his fingers into his ears, and said: Ephphatha, that is, be opened; and at once the doors of his mouth and his ears were opened. The voice found a way to burst out, and the ears found a way to hear sound. The hindrances of the tongue were put to flight, and the coverings of the ears fell away. He was found worthy [to enjoy the benefits] of the Saviour, so that he might both give thanks to the Lord with his mouth and hear the word of God from one preaching; he received faith from hearing, believed with the heart unto righteousness, and confessed with the mouth unto salvation. And what of the blind man? The blind man too is healed; he receives the brightness of sight through the hands of the Saviour: darkness yields to light, and all blindness is put to flight by the mighty works of Christ; light is restored to the one who longed for it, and having received so clear a splendour, the blind man rejoices, raises his opened eyes to heaven, and receiving sweet sight, gives thanks for everything to God: in the hands of Christ all benefits abide. Having first laid his hands on him, he asked the blind man whether he saw anything. He said: I see men like trees walking (Mark 8). His sight was still wavering, his vision still clouded. Then, having laid his hands on him again, all the confusion of darkness removed, he received clear light with sweet splendour. To him, our Lord Jesus Christ, let us always give thanks, to whom be dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
XI. Likewise, on the Gospel reading Mark 12:42.

It has been recited today that when the Lord had sat down in the temple opposite the treasury, he saw the crowds casting [money] into the treasury; and he saw the rich putting in much, and one poor little widow casting in two small coins. And calling his disciples together he said to them: Amen I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all. For all put in out of what they had in abundance; but she, out of her money, put in all the living that she had. O lover of mercy, who praises not the wealth of the rich but the straits of the poor! He commended the deed of the poor little woman above the others, and [declared] that amid the wealth of those who abound, the little is worth more: for with him it is not the quantity of money but the devotion of the mind that is approved. O blessed and righteous widow, who was found worthy to be praised before the day of judgement! She put two small coins into the treasury, and by the gift of so tiny an alms acquired a great reward; and, as it seems to me, raised up and borne aloft by these two, as if by two wings, she reached the heights. She who endured straits in the world found a place in heaven. And the Lord gave his testimony in the sight of the disciples, to prove that even a slight alms has a great reward with the Lord; which the blessed Apostle also says: He who sows generously will also reap generously; and he who sows in blessing will also reap in blessing (2 Cor. 9). For God loves a cheerful giver; for he who shows mercy will obtain mercy, and he who shares with the needy is heaped with heavenly rewards. I have been young, says David, and now am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread. All day long he shows mercy and lends, and his seed will be in blessing (Ps. 36). Hence the blessed prophet Isaiah admonishes everyone and exhorts them to works of mercy, saying: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy without a roof into your house. If you see the naked, clothe [him], and do not despise those of your own household and seed. Then your early light will break forth, and your garments will quickly spring up, and righteousness will go before you; the glory of God will surround you (Isa. 58), and so on. Therefore, brothers, out of what the Lord deigns to bestow, let us give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, hospitality to the stranger; let us offer service to the sick, comfort to the afflicted; let us work often in the treasury, as far as we are able; for the eyes of the Lord always look upon us and are always present, and in every place they watch the good and the wicked, who will each render account according to his works: to him be glory for ever. Amen.
XII. Likewise, on the Gospel reading John 11:1.

It has been recited to us today in the holy Gospel that Lazarus, four days dead, was raised by the Lord, the Saviour himself praying to the Father and saying: Father, I give you thanks that you have heard me; and I knew that you always hear me; but I said it because of the people standing round, that they may believe that you sent me; and afterwards he cried out: Lazarus, come out; and at once he who had been dead came forth, bound feet and hands with bands; and his face was bound with a cloth; and he ordered him to be untied and to go (John 11). Listen, brothers: the body of Lazarus lay dead and lifeless in the tomb, and the limp limbs, in which there had been no life for four days, were gradually decaying in the grave. Christ prays to the Father, and the dead man receives strength; he entreats the Begetter, and he is made firm. Then he cries: Lazarus, come out, and death is terrified, hell trembles, and at once at the Saviour's voice the body, quickened, is shaken loose, and the limbs wrapped in linen cloths grow warm with the motion of life. The Lord orders him to be untied and to go away, lest he be thought a phantom. He orders him untied, so that they might recognize both the bindings, now damp, and the body, and see the freshly restored limbs with their fresh pallor. The Lord showed in Lazarus a sign of the future resurrection, as also in the son of the widow and in the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue. For indeed, beloved, all the dead could have risen up together, raised at a single word of the Saviour, had he not called each one by name; therefore he said to each: Lazarus, come out; Young man, I say to you, arise. To you, he says, I say, only for the present time: you, arise. Talitha cumi, that is, girl, arise. So [he called] each one, as I said, by name. And he willed this, so that what is seen in individuals may be understood as going to happen in all generally: he is our Lord, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, whose voice all will hear; and those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, but those who [have done] evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5). To him be glory and dominion for ever. Amen.
XIII. Likewise, on the holy Gospel, Matthew 26:7.

It has been told that, while the Lord was reclining at a banquet, a certain sinful woman came, carrying an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing at the Lord's feet she wet his feet with tears, and wiped them with her hair, and kissed them, and anointed them with ointment. She did not dare thrust herself shamelessly before that most holy gaze; nor, placed as she was in the darkness of sins, could she bear his rays even a little, but she stood at his feet, worshipping the lowest part of his body, and as if under the shade of his feet she sought cooling for the burning heat of her sins; believing that he had taken a body for the remission of sins, she kissed his feet and watered them with tears and wiped them with her hair, [the feet] with which he travelled through various places and offered himself as saving light to all who were sick. So this sinful woman did penance with her eyes, her hair, and her lips, the very things by which she had chiefly contracted the vices of sins, and sought pardon. And the Lord, who always wishes to heal the sicknesses of penitents, said to her: Your sins shall be forgiven you; and again: Her many sins shall be forgiven, because she loved much (Matt. 26). O inestimable mercy! He gave back joy for weeping, and this heavenly physician heals her who was sick in her evils, so that where there had been despair over offences, there might be the security of joys. He says further: Your faith has saved you; go in peace; flee the wars of the vices, walk in the peace of chastity, of humility, of sobriety, and so on.
XIV. Likewise, on the Gospel reading, Matthew 5:14.

The Lord says: You are the light of this world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house, and so on.

So, he says to the disciples, you are the light of this world: a city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. It is certain that a city set on a mountain gives light to all, and is plain to all, and cannot be hidden. This the Lord spoke in parables as a figure of the disciples. For the city set on a mountain is understood as the soul joined in fellowship with Christ, which stands firm in him and, raised up by faith in him, stands out far and wide. The soul is called a city because in it the divine laws and rights are written: Who show, he says, the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom. 2). So a city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. Christ was called a mountain by the holy prophet Daniel: He came, he says, to the earth, and became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth (Dan. 2), growing in the minds of believers. He was also called the cornerstone, set at the head of the corner, who coupled and joined in one faith two peoples, like two walls coming from opposite directions, from the circumcision and the uncircumcision. And rightly is he at the head, because he is the head of the Church, he who is also called the foundation. For so the Apostle says: No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus (1 Cor. 3). So he is both the stone at the head and the foundation below. Why below? Because Christ is from the things above and from the things below; he is God and man, Word and flesh, living for ever, and dead for a time; one thing in Christ is impassible, another passible, one before time, another in time.

So he himself is called mountain, stone and foundation; and the rock, he says, was Christ (1 Cor. 10). On this rock every wise man builds his house, that is, the house of his soul; and the winds come, and the rain descends, and the rivers beat against that house, and it does not fall: its foundation is upon the rock. So, as we had begun to say, a city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. There follows: nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. The lamp set on the lampstand is the mind placed within the substance of the body, which shines and stands out, especially if it does not lack the oil of charity or chastity, as was that blessed John the Baptist, of whom it is written: He was a burning and shining lamp (John 5). He burned and he shone: he burned with the heat of the Holy Spirit, he shone with the light of Christ. Hear this lamp crying out about Christ and saying: This is the Lamb of God, this is he who takes away the sins of the world (John 1); and again he says: The man who comes after me was made before me; whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. So the mind of blessed John shone with the light of Christ, because from his fullness, as it is written (John 1), all the saints receive grace for grace. All the saints receive from his light, and the majesty of Christ's light is not divided into parts, is not diminished. For if the light of a lamp, when, for example, a thousand torches or a great many lamps are lit from it, that fire is not diminished, nor is it divided into parts from itself, how much more is the majesty of Christ full, and his fullness abounds in all, and is not divided, but he is whole in all. For our speech too, while it is spoken, is heard by all, and is not divided among individuals, but is whole and entire in all; and if we all read a little verse written on a wall, we do not divide it into parts, but it remains whole in the senses of each one; and therefore, brothers, the saints, shining, as we have said, always from the light of Christ, cried out saying: Or do you seek proof of him who speaks in me, Christ (2 Cor. 13)? And therefore they give light to all who are in the house, that is, in the house of this world; because in a great house, as it is written (2 Tim. 2), there are not only vessels of gold or silver, but of wood and earthenware. So all the saints are appointed for the enlightenment of men, and the apostles and prophets were appointed so that the building of the Church might be constructed through them, by the Lord's gift: to our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ himself be glory and dominion for ever. Amen.
XV. Likewise, on the holy Gospel, Matthew 17:1.

It was read in the holy Gospel thus: After six days, it says, Jesus took Peter, James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain apart, and he was transfigured before them. And his face shone like the sun; and his garments became white as snow. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him. And Peter answered and said: Master, it is good for us to be here: let us make three tabernacles here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah, and so on. After six days, it says; after six days we understand the sabbath, the seventh day. The first day is the Lord's day, the second day the second feria, and so all the days. After six days, as has been said, the sabbath is counted. This day signifies rest, because on the seventh day too God rested from his works. So on this sanctified day the Lord showed that all the saints, both in the law and in the prophets, together with the blessed apostles, would be present with him in his glory and would remain with him. Moses was the lawgiver, who described all the saints from the origin of the world; so with him all the saints will rise again. Elijah signifies the number of the prophets, and with him all the prophets; in Moses and Elijah, those who have died and been buried will be found alive, and will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. So the three apostles, Peter, James and John, [signify] those who believe with them, and also all who follow the faith of Peter, James and John. Of these it is written: Peter, James and John, who seemed to be pillars (Gal. 2); rightly called pillars, who supported the building of the Church and raised it from the lower things to the higher, so that they might seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. So there are two, Moses and Elijah, and three apostles, so that every word might stand on two and three witnesses. And the Lord himself said: Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them (Matt. 18). Here too the Lord showed that those who do not accept the law and the prophets are to be confounded, because he joined them to himself and associated them with the number of the apostles. Moses wrote about the Lord (Exod. 17), and as a type of Christ he raised his hands on the mountain against Amalek, as Christ [did] on the cross to defeat the devil. Again Elijah (3 Kings 17), in order to raise a dead man, stretched himself out, which the Lord did on the cross, to put death to flight and restore life. Let us see what follows. Saint Peter says to the Lord: It is good for us to be here: let us make three tabernacles here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. Peter [said] this out of the affection of a good disciple, who loved Moses and Elijah, the ministers and friends of the Lord. And behold, a cloud came overshadowing them, and a voice from the cloud saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; as if to say: I do not want three tabernacles to be made; but this is my most beloved Son, whose tabernacle will be one, that is, one Church, spread through the whole world, in the likeness of the one city of Jerusalem which is in heaven. In this Church Moses and Elijah, Peter, James and John will be present, always bearing witness to the Lord, with all the patriarchs and prophets and the holy apostles; with whom may we too, all who believe, always exult and glory in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, always giving thanks to the Father through him: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
XVI. Likewise, the Gospel reading, Luke 12:50.

The Lord says: I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want but that it be kindled? But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished! and so on. I came, he says, to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want but that it be kindled? The Lord casts fire onto the earth of our breast, to cultivate the field of our heart, to burn up the thorns and thistles of sins, so that the cold of our wickedness may be driven out, and by the heat of the Holy Spirit all things fruitful and prosperous may spring up in us. For take a comparison from this earthly fire; a certain author of secular literature says: Often too it has profited to set fire to barren fields, and to burn the light stubble with crackling flames; whether the lands thereby draw hidden strength and rich nourishment, or whether through the fire every taint is baked out of them and the useless moisture sweats away; or whether that heat opens more paths and loosens hidden pores, by which the sap may come to the new blades; or whether it rather hardens and binds tight the gaping veins. If this earthly and bodily fire achieves and effects this, how much more that heavenly and holy fire, which so penetrates the recesses of the soul that, passing also through the whole substance of the body, it renders the whole man clean and fruitful; and this fire produces in a man as many fruits as the apostle Paul sets out, saying: The fruit of the Spirit, of that fiery spirit, is charity, joy, peace, patience, goodness, faith (Gal. 5), etc. Charity, he says, at the head, because the cold of iniquity never extinguishes the fire of charity; so again divine Scripture says: Much water does not extinguish charity, and rivers will not overwhelm it (Song 8), [...]. I came, he says, to cast fire upon the earth: and what do I want but that it be kindled? It is kindled through good will, through a good resolve of the mind, which in a certain way increases and inflames that divine fire within itself. This fire is further kindled in us by the frequent breath of the divine Scriptures; and so the holy Apostle, knowing this, instructed his disciple Timothy, saying: Attend to yourself and to reading; persevere in them. For in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you (1 Tim. 4). And the fire, he says, will save you, shining with its healthfulness, and you will enlighten the others who hear you. Then the Lord went on, saying: But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished (Luke 12)! This the Lord said about his passion. He further added, saying: Do you think that I came to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but separation. For from now on five in one house will be divided, three against two, and two against three: father against son, and son against his father; mother against daughter, and daughter against her mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (ibid.). This division is made by the faithful against the unfaithful. For when some consent to the faith of the Lord and others dissent, they are separated by faith; and this separation saves believers but condemns unbelievers. For it is just that the faithful should depart, because there can be no fellowship of light with darkness, nor can sweet be mixed with bitter, nor the faithful with the unfaithful. And therefore, brothers, persevering in the faith of the Lord, let us strive both to lead unbelievers to the faith of the Lord and that all of us may be saved in Christ: to whom be glory and dominion for ever. Amen.
XVII. Likewise, on the Gospel reading, Mark 2:15.

The passage was read where the Lord is said to have held a banquet at the house of Levi with tax-collectors and sinners. The Lord did not keep tax-collectors and sinners away, so that they might be taught, if only on the occasion of a banquet. He who was just and holy did not drive away the ungodly and unjust, for he had come to heal all, as he himself had said: It is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are unwell (Matthew 9). On those who were caught in the many fevers of desires he poured the sweet refreshment of his words. There was an abundance of food and drink; but the Saviour, seeing them intent on these things, joined them at an earthly banquet, so that he might urge them to hasten to the heavenly banquets, where there are those delights, not temporal but eternal, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him (Isaiah 64 and 1 Corinthians 2). It is not, he says, the healthy who need a physician, but those who are unwell. You who are sick in soul, held by whatever disease of vices; you who have fevers of pride, or of lust, or of evil desire, or of anger, or of avarice, run to Christ the physician and, entreating him, say to him: I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you (Psalm 40); so that he too may say [...] if you hear my words [...] [...] and [...] you will feel the medicine, the help of divine aid, if you bring the devotion of your mind to the divine precepts with complete observance. It is a great and good thing, brothers, to obey the heavenly command; and salvation is gained there where hearing serves obedience. Therefore let us obey the divine precepts, so that, having obtained the substance of good things, we may always give thanks to the Father through the Son: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
XVIII. Likewise, on the holy Gospel, Luke 4:12

We heard read today in the holy Gospel about two sons, a younger and an elder, among whom their father had divided his property; and how the younger, going abroad far from his father and living wantonly in sins, lost everything, and afterwards, led by repentance and much afflicted, returned to his father; and the father ordered that a robe and a ring and shoes be given him, and that a calf be killed for a banquet for his redemption [...] [...] coming [...] consoling him [...]: Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was right to feast and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found. These two brothers, as it seems to my littleness, dearest ones, carry the meaning of two peoples. The elder can be understood as the ancient people of the patriarchs or prophets, who persevered with God the Father, serving him; the younger, as the people of the Gentiles, who, distancing themselves from God as if setting out abroad, lived in many errors, and who afterwards, coming to the father repentant and entreating, received the first robe, that is, the first adornment of redemption; for it is written: You Gentiles shall be at the head (Deuteronomy 24). The ring on the hand is the sign of betrothal; and the bride, according to the Apostle, betrothed to one husband, is presented as a chaste virgin; the shoes on the feet, this too is for a sign of the wedding, since the feet of the bride of Christ are shod in preparation of the Gospel of peace. A calf too is ordered to be killed for the banquet. The fatted calf is our Saviour himself, whom the Father willed to be sacrificed for the redemption of the human race. As for what is said, that the elder brother was angry on account of the younger brother, there anger stands for wonder; for the ancient people of the just wondered at the reception of the Gentiles. And although some of these were truly angry, that is, the peoples of the Jews, nevertheless they are admonished by the divine precepts that they ought to rejoice, because the small understanding of human frailty ought to accept kindly the counsel of God's indulgence. Therefore let the people of the Gentiles, converted to the Lord, rejoice that they have been saved by the Lord's kindness, and always give thanks to God the Father through his Christ: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
XIX. The reading of the holy Gospel, Luke 16:19.

We heard read today in the holy Gospel: There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day; and there was a certain beggar named Eleazar, who lay at his gate full of sores, longing to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. And the dogs too came and licked his sores. And it came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And lifting up his eyes when he was in torments, he saw Abraham far off, and Eleazar in his bosom; and he cried out and said: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Eleazar to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. And Abraham said to him: Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Eleazar likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor cross over from there to here.

Let us consider, brothers, that a rich man and a beggar are set forth. The rich man's name is passed over in silence, and he is without a name, like a body without a head: the name is recognized in the head; he is rightly without a name, because he was without a head, he who had in himself neither faith in Christ, who is the head, nor mercy. Then the beggar is named Eleazar, and his name is contained in the book of Life, which is why it is not passed over in silence in the Gospel either. I. That rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day also died, and was buried in hell. II. But Eleazar the beggar died and, carried by angels, was placed in Abraham's bosom. III. The judgement of God was shown at once in both: the poor man received, after many labours and pains, the refreshment he had longed for; the rich man too received, after his arrogance, fitting torments; hence the rich man, when he saw Eleazar resting in Abraham's bosom, cried out and said: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Eleazar to dip the tip of his finger, to cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. And Abraham said to him: Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Eleazar likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. The rich man sought to be touched by the dew of the tip of Eleazar's finger, and it was not permitted him, for it is written: In death who will be mindful of you; and in hell who will confess to you (Psalm 6)? And now, if the rich are willing, let them take care of the poor; they have and see many Eleazars; when they show them mercy, they prepare refreshment for themselves in the future, for whoever shows mercy will obtain mercy. For one who has not himself been merciful will not be able to deserve God's mercy; let them rather humble themselves in prosperity; arrogance has [...] [...] [...] of the world, above all not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us with all things. Hence the Apostle teaches [them] to be rich in good works, to be generous, ready to give, sharing, storing up for themselves a good treasure for the future, so that they may lay hold of true life (1 Timothy 6). There are many rich people who are not blameworthy, who seem to hold what they possess not for themselves alone but for many; they give generously to many with piety, they distribute well to many. He is truly rich in God who gives to the sighing poor man, and not to the dancing actor. There are many rich bishops, and presbyters, and deacons; but whoever dispenses his riches well will be able to have neither the guilt of luxury, nor the mark of crime, nor the penalty of damnation. Indeed, God willed some to be rich for this reason, that there may be those who give to the poor; and for this reason he made [some] poor, that they may receive necessities from the rich. For the counsel of God is holy in all things, to be revered in every way, and always to be praised: to God the Father himself be glory always, for ever. Amen.
XX. Likewise, on the reading of the holy Gospel, Mark 8:5.

Behold, he says, the sower went out to sow, etc. The Lord Jesus came into the world, having gone out from the Father himself, saying: I came forth from the Father and have come into this world; again I leave the world and go to the Father (John 16). So he says of himself: Behold, the sower went out to sow. He went out, then, to sow the Gospel in the world, to sow faith, justice, truth, peace, chastity, humility and the other virtues. And the devil, on the contrary, began to sow his own things, that is, pride, anger, lust, murders, adulteries, thefts and the other vices, which in the divine writings are called tares. For when the disciples said to the Lord Jesus: Did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then does it have tares? The Saviour says: An enemy has done this (Matthew 13); calling the devil himself the enemy of man, who sends in enmities between God and men, that is, sins, by which he may separate men from God. For it was he who, changed into the form of a serpent with slippery coils, beguiled those first humans too, Adam and Eve, placed in paradise, with speech as if of a man, and deceived their untried souls through incautious credulity. He it is who now too sends in wicked thoughts, which will burn with him at the judgement of Christ. And therefore let us consider, brothers, the seeds of the Lord Jesus Christ and the seeds of the enemy, the devil. For when each one sees rising in his heart thoughts and desires of piety, mercy, humility, chastity, patience and the other good things, let him know that they are seeds of Christ. But if [he sees] desire for adultery, fornication, theft, fraud and the other evils, let him understand that they are seeds of the devil. And therefore let him prepare his heart for God, and not for the devil, as the prophet says in the Psalms: My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and play psalms to you in your glory (Psalm 56); as I have received the seeds of your justifications, I offer you fruits of praise and blessing. Behold, he says, the sower went out to sow; and while he sows, some fell beside the road, some on rocky ground, some among thorns, some on good ground. As for what [fell] beside the road, the birds come and take it away. Whoever does not walk on the road, which is Christ, being placed off the road, will not be able to hold within himself the seed of the word of God; but it is snatched away by the birds, that is, by wandering spirits. But whoever has a rocky mind, that is, hardness weighed down by faithlessness, does not keep in himself the roots of the word of God; but it quickly withers, because it does not produce lasting fruits from the depths of the heart. And what [fell] among thorns is choked by the thickness of the thorns, that is, by the prickings of worldly thoughts, which press down the word, and it cannot become fruitful. But what [fell] on good ground abounds in fruits and grows to plenty, so that it bears, as the Lord says, fruits thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold; fruits of hope, faith, charity; fruits of widowhood, virginity, martyrdom. With these fruits the Church grows well, and worthily prepares its harvests for the heavenly granaries, as is said generally of all the prophets, or apostles, or various teachers. Hence the Lord says well: Whoever speaks sows the word. And so it is, since whoever speaks the word scatters words like seeds, but God gives the increase. For the apostle Paul too said: We have sown spiritual things for you (1 Corinthians 9). Since, then, whoever speaks sows the word, and just as seed, when it is cast on the ground, drenched by heavenly rain, takes root and grows in the hearts of each; and from it come those fruits which are called those of good will, both thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.
XXI. Likewise, on the Gospel reading, Mark 7:25.

The Lord Jesus, it says, entered a house and wanted no one to know, and he could not be hidden, etc. First let us consider what this means, brothers: The Lord, it says, entered a house and wanted no one to know, and he could not be hidden. For if he wanted no one to know, why could he not be hidden? Surely the Lord does not wish to show himself in such a way that he yet wishes to be hidden. For is it because the divine substance is not now seen by our eyes that it is therefore absent from us, or does not wish to be present to us? For he himself pours the light of his knowledge into all, he who is the true light, enlightening every man coming into this world. He entered a house, but he was not absent from public places either; he was in the body, but he was not missing from heaven; he was seen ... ... of whom he speaks in the psalm through the prophet David, saying: Who stretches out the heaven like a skin, who has touched its upper parts in the waters; who makes the clouds his ascent, who walks upon the wings of the winds, who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire (Psalm 103). Therefore it is he who with the Father founded the world. There came to him, it says, a certain woman, a Syrophoenician, a gentile by race, and she asked him to cast the demon out of her daughter (Mark 7:25). This woman, to speak allegorically, was both the gentile error and the ancient ignorance, which had borne a daughter subject to a demon, a wretched and weak offspring, which did not have a manly sense, that is, one strong in faith, but one slack in faithlessness. When this woman, running to the Lord, asked him, the Saviour said: It is not good to take the children's bread and give it to the dogs. But she answered and said: Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their master's table (Mark 7). She compared herself to little dogs sighing at their masters' table. She not only humbled herself to the master, but even before the servants and children of the master she compared herself to puppies. And the Lord [said] to her: Go, he said; because of this saying the demon will go out of your daughter. You see, then, that if anyone comes to Christ from the error of the gentiles, and acknowledges him as Lord and Saviour, he will both benefit himself and gain salvation for his children, so that, freed from the power of demons, they may obtain the reward of liberation. Next it was read that the Lord put his fingers into the ears of a certain deaf and dumb man, and touched his tongue with his spittle, and at once he spoke and recovered his hearing. Nothing is impossible to God (Romans 10); whatever he touches is made strong, whatever he looks upon will live; the tongue felt, the ears felt the kindness of their Lord, they were rid of their impediments, they received use from their inertness ... ... Ephphatha, that is, be opened; at the Lord's command the benefits followed, the bond of the tongue was loosed; with his own spittle he touched his tongue: from the substance of his own flesh he bestowed health; with the fingers of his hands, again, he poured hearing into the ears. Through the members the power of the Godhead was at work. He himself now too makes the deaf hear, that is, unbelievers believe, because faith [comes] from hearing, and hearing through the word of God; [he makes] the dumb speak: those who did not know how to speak the word of truth he makes teachers and masters in the Church, preachers of the truth, so that they too may penetrate the ears of others with teaching and open them by piercing them through, and may make the tongues of their hearers eloquent too, and all, strengthened in the unity of faith, may rejoice always in the Lord Jesus Christ himself, to whom is glory and dominion for ever. Amen.
XXII. Likewise, on the reading of the Gospel, Mark 8, from verse 1 to 26.

It was said today, when the holy Gospel was read, that the Lord Jesus Christ fed the people with seven loaves and a few fishes, and that seven hampers full of fragments were gathered. The heavenly King, our Lord Jesus Christ, feeds his people both from the land and from the sea. With seven loaves all are filled. Why, do we think, was this number written of the loaves? I think that by the gift of Christ's grace seven Churches were established, through whose sevenfold number all peoples are fed in Christ; and seven full hampers are left over as well, because the grace of the Churches is never diminished, but they are always heaped up by the bounty of the Holy Spirit. This sevenfold Church holds in itself a perfect number, just as seven days are completed in the perfecting of the world, and seven thousand years are said to be appointed until the consummation of the world itself. For in the Apocalypse too (chapter 5) seven eyes of the Lord are spoken of, which watch over the world, and seven stars in the hands of God. So the seven full hampers are shown to be left over, so that the Churches may be known to be always full of the grace of Christ. Likewise, in what follows, it is said of the blind man who was given light that the Lord Jesus Christ, again seeing a man blind from his birth, cured him thus: He spat, it says, on his eyes, and laid his hand on him, and asked him whether he saw anything; and he said: I see men like trees walking. And again he laid on his hand, and he saw all things clearly. This blind man, to whom his birth had not given light, but who had suffered the shipwreck of his sight at his very birth, now obtains healing from the Lord: the true light of our Saviour, who enlightened his eyes and his darkness, removed the captivity of his sight, granted the sight of free light. Struck by the rush of light after long darkness, at first, with wavering eyes, he saw as it were trees walking; then, repeated ... ... ...
XXIII. Fragment on these words: The names of the twelve apostles are these: first Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, and the rest, Matthew 10:3.

... as first ... they received ... this one first received ... Simon, who is called Peter; son ... and Israel names enumerat[ed] ... Moses did not say first ... in simple speech ... Simon ... all; but now, showing great ...ence and singular honour to blessed Peter, the Evangelist says: First Simon, who is called Peter, and Peter is interpreted 'clothed over', over what is in the law [being] the purity of grace, because he was shepherd of the Church, and moreover shepherd of the flock. For Jesus said to him: Feed my sheep (John 21). Disciple, therefore, and foundation of the Church, and apostle, and moreover martyr, he was crucified at Rome head downwards: for all these things he was crowned twofold. Therefore Peter is fittingly interpreted 'clothed over'. Andrew his brother is interpreted 'obstructed' ... guardians then ... is interpreted 'surrounded' ... ... ... pain, for in which ... death, and he despised pain. When his head was cut off by Herod ... in this he got around the ... unjust devil himself, when he passed swiftly from this world into the heavenly kingdoms; and John his brother. For John is interpreted 'obedient to the Lord'. And who obeyed the Lord as John himself did, who was bidden to follow him, and reclined on the Lord's breast? He too, with James, was surnamed son of thunder, as one who would thunder at the last in the holy Church with spiritual and heavenly power. After these, Philip, who is interpreted 'confounded, yet living'; whence Paul too says: We have been made a spectacle to this world; and like refuse ... ... Now Bartholomew too is interpreted 'dearest son'. For this reason he called him to the apostolate, and ... named him dearest son. Would that we all ... might live in the adoption of sons, so as to be numbered among the dearest sons of God. Then Thomas, who is interpreted 'abyss', or 'deep', or 'unsearchable', as a vessel of the Holy Spirit, as a temple of the Paraclete, who searches all things, who seeks out all the depths in the things that have been made, both in angels and in men. And Matthew, who is interpreted 'gift of life'. For the most magnificent Matthew became a twofold gift of life to this world: both in that [he was] an apostle, and in that [he was] an evangelist; for the Hebrews, singularly, he wrote this Gospel in Hebrew, and for the gentiles singularly, through which this Gospel was announced to the gentiles. But, it says, Matthew the tax-collector ... from your father, or from your grandfather, or from your region ... nation you name. But yourself, O blessed Matthew, from the tax-collector: why do you accuse Matthew, O blessed evangelist? Why do you rebuke the evangelist? O blessed apostle and most true disciple of the Lord, why do you not spare yourself? I, he says, Matthew, am called an evangelist, and I am most certainly an apostle. I do not, then, accuse Matthew, but much rather magnify [him], that he from a tax-collector should become an apostle; nor do I rebuke the evangelist, but rather praise [him] as a wonderful herald of the truth. It is not so wonderful, then, that someone should be good among the good, but this is exceedingly glorious, that someone should be shown good among the wicked. I name myself a tax-collector, of course, so that all may believe that this writing of mine is most true, and [my] preaching without flattery ... for I do not speak about myself ... I should speak. If I do not speak to flatter myself, how shall I speak to flatter him about whom I make this preaching, that is, about the Only-begotten God? Matthew the tax-collector. And James of Alphaeus, which is interpreted 'they will get around doctrine'; not only he, but also all the blessed apostles through spiritual doctrine got around first the devil, then all the wise of this world. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. Thaddaeus was at the beginning called Lebbaeus by his parents, which is 'heart', discipline, mind; he received an increase of this name when he was called by the Lord Thaddaeus, which is 'praise of life', as one praising eternal life to many, or praising and evangelizing the Lord himself, who is the eternal life of all. Then Simon the Canaanite, which is 'obedience', or 'prepared', as blessed Simon was, and all the apostles, both obedient and prepared. Therefore he swiftly obeyed the Lord, and readily followed after him, as the others did. And we ought to be, dearest brothers, obedient and prepared ... need for good speech ... walking in the footsteps of the most blessed apostles, we may obtain rest on the day of hiding. But let us not pass over Judas either, since the blessed evangelist did not omit [him]. Judas, it says, Iscariot, who also betrayed him, last of all, after all, worthily and fittingly, as if preparing this for himself, as if providing this for himself; and not only is this great, that he is named last, but it is infinite long-suffering that he should be named here at all. Judas, it says; which is interpreted 'freely confessed'. What did he confess? That he betrayed just blood. I have sinned, he says, in that I have betrayed just blood (Matthew 27). You yourself confess, O Judas; but you confess late, you confess badly. Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him: not only, of course, is he himself confounded and dishonoured because of his evil daring, but also his province and his region in which he was born, which is called Scarioth, is named on his account, suffers rebuke and bears a curse, because it produced such a man. Just as, then, the provinces and nations of the saints are magnificently exalted and honoured because of them, so too those of the unjust are recalled through the generations, to the greater rebuke of those who sprang from there. These twelve apostles Jesus now sent to enlighten what was dark, to correct what was crooked, to seek out what was lost, to enlighten this world, and to turn all into the way of life. These twelve Jesus sent to teach all religion, to enlighten all with faith, to commend to all the singular sovereignty of the unbegotten Father, to show to all the obedience of this Son who was sent, to manifest to all the singular illumination of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete. These twelve, then, Jesus sent, commanding them and saying: Do not go into the way of the gentiles, and do not walk into the cities of the Samaritans (Matthew 13).
